slides.title: Combustion Spark Ignition Engines (SI)
slides.body:
CombustionSpark
Spark advance (RESPECT TO TDC):
- Combustion does not start immediately after spark plug ignition. ADVANCE
- An higher spark advance increases the peak pressure (and temperatures), thus power and
efficiency (typical 15°/25° before TDC).
- Increases engine mechanical and thermal stresses and might lead to engine knock unless higher
OCTANE NUMBER (typical 95 ÷ 100 for gasoline, up to >120 for methane) fuels are used.
Influence of the compression ratio:
- Higher compression ratios lead to higher efficiency
- Increases engine mechanical and thermal stresses and might lead to engine knock and self
ignition unless higher OCTANE NUMBER fuels are used.
- Reducing the spark advance may be necessary in order to avoid the aforementioned
phenomena (thus reducing efficiency)
- Turbocharged engines generally use lower compression ratios (thus reducing efficiency).

slides.title: Misfire , Knock and Pre - ignition Spark Ignition Engines (SI)
slides.body:
Misfire, Knock and Pre-ignitionSpark
Misfire: the fuel is too much diluted in the intake air. Combustion cannot occur.
Unburned fuel is exhausted (pollutants).
Choke: the fuel is too little diluted in the intake air. Combustion cannot occur.
Unburned fuel is exhausted (pollutants).
Knock: the combustion is triggered by
some other hot spot (e.g. the exhaust
valve) in the combustion chamber after
the start of combustion by the spark plug
(the flame fronts collide).
Pre-ignition: the combustion is triggered by some other hot spot (e.g. the exhaust valve) in
the combustion chamber before the start of combustion by the spark plug.
May be caused by overheating or by a too high compression ratio (the mixture
overheats by effect of the compression before the spark ignition).

slides.title: A quick comparison Diesel vs SI
slides.body:
A quick comparisonDiesel vs SI
The intake is free, there is no throttle body.
The air flow mainly depends on engine
speed only (rpm).
As a consequence, diesel engines ALWAYS
operate with excess air.
The combustion occurs along the
expansion stroke (slower than SI
engines)
There is no spark plug, the combustion
starts spontaneously for the high pressures
and temperatures at the end of the
compression stroke (typical end of
compression pressures are around
60bars 120-130bar, 2x of SI engines).
In order to attain the higher pressure and
temperatures, the compression ratio is
higher than SI engines (𝟏𝟓 ÷ 𝟐𝟎)
Diesel fuel is not very volatile. It is
injected at extremely high pressures (up
to 2000bars) in order to form small droplets

slides.title: M ain C haracteristics Diesel engines
slides.body:
Main CharacteristicsDiesel
The mixture is dishomogeneous within the
combustion chamber: the AFR varies from
0 in fuel droplets to infinity in areas where
air only is instantaneously present.
The shorter the ignition delay, the better the fuel
quality. The CETANE NUMBER defines the fuel
quality (typically 51 ÷ 60). With shorter ignition
delay, higher engine speeds can be obtained.
Fuel is injected when the pressure and
temperature conditions to trigger combustion
are already present, the combustion starts
after a temperature dependent ignition
delay after injection.
The air mass in the combustion chamber is
approximately the same (differently from SI engines
where the throttle modulates the density). Torque and
thus power regulation is obtained by directly varying
the quantity of injected fuel.
The combustion mechanism is mainly diffusive
rather than premixed (as in SI engines)
The absence of throttle (less pumping losses) and
higher compression ratio, allow higher efficiencies
compared to SI engines.

slides.title: Combustion 1/2 Diesel engines
slides.body:
Combustion 1/2Diesel
As combustion progresses, the fuel drop evaporates (reduces its size),
producing more fuel vapours.
If the oxygen concentration at the reaction zone gets too low, the combustion
may stop (e.g. for poor jet mixing, low turbolence)→A fuel droplet surface is
partially oxidized because of the high temperature (carbonization), producing
soot.
Soot is also produced when the temperature is too high (the fuel drop surface is
carbonized before it vaporizes completely.
The smaller the fuel droplets are, the easier it
gets for it to vaporize completely, thus limiting
soot formation.

slides.title: Diesel engines Combustion 2/2
slides.body:
Analogously to spark advance for SI engines,
increasing the injection advance in Diesel engines
increases peak pressure and temperature (thus
efficiency), but mechanical and thermal stresses are
increased (and engine noise).
Same considerations as SI engines apply.
The ignition delay is extremely sensitive with temperature, 200𝐾
temperature difference may increase the ignition delay by 20 times
(logarithmic time scale in figure).
Glow plugs are used for cold start in diesel engines, in order to
create a ‘’hot spot’’ where combustion can start more easily

slides.title: Soot production Observations NOx production Observations Diesel engines Pollutants
slides.body:
- Too little oxygen (locally or globally)
- Poor air-fuel mixing (low turbolence)
- Poor vaporization (droplets too large)
- Temperature too low (too low injection advance)
- In some soot can be produced even when
temperature is too high
- Soot is basically unburnt fuel, its presence
indicates low efficiency
- One of the main causes of soot production is
low in-chamber temperature
- Atmospheric air is made up of ~79% of molecular Nitrogen
(𝑁2) and ~21% Oxygen (𝑂2).
- Molecular nitrogen is usually an inert gas at low
temperatures.
- 𝑁2 and 𝑂2, because of the high temperatures and longer
combustion times of Diesel engines, decompose to their
atomic form 𝑁 and 𝑂.
- This is particularly true for Diesel engines where the excess
air is far higher than SI engines.
- Atomic nitrogen can be oxydixed and form the so-called NOx
(nitrous oxydes)→𝑁𝑂 and 𝑁𝑂2.
- NOx are basically due to the high efficiency of Diesel engines: high
temperatures and pressures and no throttling (excess air).

slides.title: Diesel engines Indirect Injectio n
slides.body:
Indirect Injection
Combustion starts more easily and more rapidly in a small volume (initial combustion
heat is more concentrated). Reduced ignition delay.
The shape of the prechamber and connecting hole, create a turbolent flow that
improved the air-burning mixture mixing.
The combustion pre-chamber slowed down the heat release (and, subsequently the
pressure) peak, reducing mechanical stresses and engine noise.
The slower heat release and larger surface exposed to the combustion heat, reduced
efficiency
The prechamber connecting hole, induce a further pressure (and thus energy) drop that
reduces efficiency.
The combustion pre-chamber strongly mitigates the requirement of having very exact
injection timing (a simpler fuel injection system may be used)

slides.title: Diesel engines Common rail injection
slides.body:
The common rail decouples the available fuel pressure
from the pressure provided by the injection pump, acting
as an hydraulic accumulator.
Since fuel is always available at high pressure, an
electronic injection system allows multiple injection in a
very short time interval (in the order of 1-2ms)
The rail pressure is electronically controlled by ECM

slides.title: Diesel engines Injection phases
slides.body:
PILOT
Reduce ignition delay of the
main injection (raises the in-
chamber temperature).
The reduced ignition delay
greatly improves combustion
noise and reduces mechanical
stresses.
PRE
Reduces oxygen availability at the
time of the main injection, reduces
NOx production but increases
soot.
AFTER
Promotes soot oxidation by
sustaining the combustion process
longer in the expansion stroke
POST
This injection is not always present.
It’s needed for the correct operation
of the aftertreatment systems (DPF).
MAIN
The time shape of this injection phase
may be varied thanks to electronically
controlled injectors
